title: Extreme conservation and rare evolutionary deviations in mammalian NOTCH3 inform the interpretation of CADASIL pathogenicity
abstract: Background/Objectives: NOTCH3 is a highly conserved transmembrane receptor whose pathogenic variants cause CADASIL, a hereditary cerebral small vessel disease characterized by vascular smooth muscle cell degeneration and extracellular NOTCH3 accumulation. Most established CADASIL variants alter cysteine residues within the extracellular EGF like repeats, but the influence of residue position, disulfide connectivity, surrounding sequence, and domain context on NOTCH3 structure and pathogenicity remains incompletely understood. We used comparative mammalian analysis to identify rare changes within conserved NOTCH3 regions and evaluate their potential relevance to disease associated molecular mechanisms. Methods: NOTCH3 protein sequences from 113 mammalian species were ana-lysed using multiple sequence alignment together with complementary structural modelling, intrinsic disorder prediction, stability, aggregation propensity, solvent-accessibility, and molecular dynamics analyses. Results: NOTCH3 showed exceptional overall conservation, including all 204 extracellular cysteine positions across nearly all species examined. Three rare sequence configurations were identified: seven cysteine substitutions and one cysteine deletion in jaguar EGFr13,14,15; an NRR deletion in Brandt bat predicted to increase S2 cleavage-site accessibility; and an exon 16 associated X1 deletion affecting EGFr20,22, previously reported in a human CADASIL pedigree and also found in selected mammals. Computational analyses predicted distinct structural consequences, including disruption of the ca-nonical disulfide framework and increased intrinsic disorder across the affected jaguar EGFr13,14,15 region, increased S2 cleavage-site accessibility in Brandt bat, and a potential compensatory disulfide rearrangement with increased aggregation propensity in the X1 deletion isoform. Conclusions: These findings provide a comparative molecular pathology framework for interpreting NOTCH3 variation beyond cysteine number alone. They support a context dependent model in which residue position, disulfide architecture, surrounding sequence, domain organization, aggregation propensity, and proteolytic regulation jointly influence the predicted structural and functional consequences of NOTCH3 variants. title: EndoMT: An R Package Resource for Endothelial-Mesenchymal Transition Gene Set Enrichment Analysis
abstract: Introduction: Endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndoMT) is a dynamic endothelial cell-state transition increasingly implicated in fibrosis, vascular dysfunction, inflammation and cancer. Despite expansion of EndoMT-focused transcriptomic research, EndoMT representation remains limited to broader epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) frameworks in standard gene set repositories. Methods: To address the absence of a general-purpose EndoMT gene set for transcriptomic enrichment analysis, we developed an open EndoMT gene set resource and accompanying R package. A literature-informed EndoMT gene set was curated and directionally assigned to EndoMT UP and EndoMT DOWN signatures according to reported or hypothesised expression during partial EndoMT, defined here as an active transitional state rather than a complete mesenchymal endpoint, to improve capture of EndoMT-associated transcriptional changes across different stages of the process. Genes were annotated by marker subtype and implemented as Gene Matrix Transposed files distributed through the R package, together with exported R objects and gene-level metadata. Benchmarking was performed using bulk RNA-seq data sets GSE118446, comprising seven-day IL-1l{beta}/TGF-{beta}2-treated human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and human pulmonary arterial endothelial cells, and GSE342578, comprising three-day TGF-{beta}1/2/3-treated HUVECs; single-cell RNA-seq data set GSE237895, comprising seven-day TGF-{beta}1-treated and SNAI1-overexpressing HUVECs; and endothelial cell and cancer-associated fibroblast populations from human metastatic melanoma single-cell RNA-seq data set GSE72056. Results: In GSE118446, EndoMT UP was positively enriched and EndoMT DOWN negatively enriched in chronically IL-1{beta}/TGF-{beta}2-treated endothelial cells, concordant with experimentally validated EndoMT induction, while partial EndoMT-associated enrichment was detected in single ligand-treatment. In contrast, EndoMT UP was negatively enriched following acute TGF-{beta}1/2/3 treatment, suggesting temporal differences between acute TGF-{beta} stimulation and chronic EndoMT induction. In GSE237895 mesenchymal-like endothelial cells, EndoMT UP was positively enriched and EndoMT DOWN negatively enriched in both TGF-{beta}1-treated and SNAI1-overexpressing models. EndoMT gene sets also discriminated endothelial and mesenchymal/stromal transcriptional states in GSE72056 metastatic melanoma. Marker subtype and Gene Ontology Biological Process analyses provided additional exploratory resolution of EndoMT-associated components beyond MSigDB Hallmark EMT. Discussion: The EndoMT R package provides a dedicated, accessible and interoperable resource for EndoMT-focused transcriptomic enrichment analysis. Benchmarking demonstrates utility for detecting established, partial and divergent EndoMT-associated states, supporting broad applicability across EndoMT biology research.

title: PowerFit: An updated framework for fast rigid-body fitting into cryo-EM density maps.
abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has become a central method for determining structures of molecular assemblies, requiring reliable tools to interpret the density maps. Despite recent advances in AI-driven model building, at intermediate-to-low resolution (4-15 [a]) accurate rigid-body fitting of existing atomic structures into cryo-EM maps remains an essential step in the modelling process. Here we present an updated version of our software package PowerFit. It performs an exhaustive translational and rotational search against the cryo-EM density map, implementing sensitive correlation functions. The updated release preserves the fitting accuracy and sensitivity of the original method while substantially improving the computational performance through modernised CPU and GPU implementations. In addition, to facilitate the interpretation of results, it provides an HTML report with interactive 3D visualisation using MolViewSpec. The same HTML report is used to generate the result page when using PowerFit via its web service. The report enables immediate inspection and validation of the results. The software's accessibility has been enhanced by updating it from Python 2 to Python 3, enabling straightforward installation via the Python Package Index (PyPI) and simple integration into computational pipelines. PowerFit is freely available at https://github.com/haddocking/powerfit, as a web service at https://wenmr.science.uu.nl/powerfit or in JupyterLite directly in a web browser at https://www.bonvinlab.org/powerfit/jupyterlite.html.

title: methylTFR: Computational quantification of transcription factor activity from DNA methylation
abstract: DNA methylation modulates transcription factor (TF) binding, and plays an important role in regulating gene expression. We developed methylTFR, an R package for quantifying TF activity from DNA methylation across TF-binding sites, providing a low-dimensional and interpretable activity profile. Across 147 human immune cell methylomes, methylTFR identified cell-type-specific regulators, including CEBP and ETS family activity in myeloid cells. In CD4+ T cells, TF activity scores resolved the naive-to-memory trajectory and highlighted AP-1 factors as important memory regulators. We applied methylTFR to sparse single-cell methylome data, and we integrated derived activity scores with gene expression and accessibility into joint factor models yielding multimodal views of lineage regulators.

title: Verification Debt in Automated Biological Research Workflows: A Proof-of-Concept
abstract: Recent biological research has shown significant interest and progress towards adoption of agentic AI systems. Domain specific agentic platforms with access to large collections of biological tools with code generation and/or querying capabilities, such as Biomni (illustrative case in point), are representative of the capability to orchestrate automated research workflows. Such platforms enable collaborative AI workspace for drug discovery, genomics, bioinformatics, literature research, and experimental planning for biologists and researchers. When such platforms are used for the aforementioned workflows, individually validating every agentic decision and the research process by which it was reached becomes challenging due to the scale of decisions involved and oftentimes, insufficient disclosure of assumptions and methodological choices, limited traceability of evidence, and interpretive judgments embedded throughout the workflow, giving rise to verification debt. Verification debt in agentic environments could result in unexpected failures and consequences in downstream experiments. This study focuses on empirical qualitative characterization of verification debt in agentic (prompt to outcomes) workflows. Biomni was chosen the testing AI agentic platform in this study mainly due to the descriptive traces it provides to track every agentic step. Verification debt is examined through two complementary angles: the individual agentic decision steps that carry claims and evidence, and the underlying research process by which the agent arrives at and reports them. This study attempts to characterize verification debt with 10 test cases (covering proteomics, genomics and drug discovery) with varying degree of biological nuance across three identical and independent runs. Verification debt is represented through 9 decision-step metrics and 13 research-process metrics, and also propose the VERIFY framework for evaluating scientific verifiability and validity in agentic workflows.

title: PIE: Generalizing perturbation effects across unseen perturbations, contexts and datasets
abstract: Predicting cellular response to perturbations is key to understanding biological mechanisms and selecting therapeutic targets. However, generalizing across cellular contexts, perturbations, and experimental datasets remains challenging due to incomplete representations of the system being perturbed and the difficulty of measuring true perturbation effects within that system. We introduce PIE, a model that addresses these limitations by reformulating the learning task around population level perturbation effects and incorporating auxiliary inputs that better characterize the biological system. PIE directly predicts differentially expressed genes and changes in gene expression for each (context, perturbation) pair, using external biological knowledge, baseline gene expression, and observed perturbation responses. Its architecture accommodates input sources with variable feature sets and predicts effects on genes seen and unseen during training. On the Replogle Nadig dataset, PIE achieves state of the art performance on most metrics across all tested generalization settings, including the most challenging setting where both the context and perturbation are unseen during training. For predicting differentially expressed genes, PIE achieves 1.2 to 3.2 times the AUPRC of the strongest baseline in each setting: across unseen contexts, perturbations, experimental datasets, and jointly unseen contexts and perturbations. Overall, PIE provides a framework for generalizing perturbation effects across diverse experimental conditions.

title: DE-SWAN analysis of biomarker trajectories over the life course is highly sensitive to age distribution and model parameterization
abstract: DE-SWAN is a commonly used method to study how large ensembles of omics biomarkers change across the life course. It has been used to demonstrate apparent repeated accelerations and decelerations of aging rates across the life course, including 2-3 peaks of aging-related changes. This result contradicts what is expected based on the demography of aging and known biological mechanisms. Here, we use simulations to study the robustness of DE-SWAN to the age distribution of the study sample and to choice of window size. We show that under many realistic scenarios, DE-SWAN is highly sensitive to factors unrelated to the underlying rates of change in aging biology. This calls into question the results of previous analyses that have attributed DE-SWAN peaks to acceleration and deceleration of aging. We conclude that the method is unreliable for studying rates of change across the life course under most circumstances.

title: Embodied mechanical sensing through self-generated motion in climbing plants
abstract: Embodied mechanical intelligence and morphological computation enable adaptive behavior by shifting computation from centralized control to body mechanics. Yet how dynamical material structures encode environmental information remains poorly understood. Here, we address this question using climbing plants as a minimal decentralized system. Combining force measurements with physical modeling, we show that circumnutating shoots generate predictable forces against candidate supports, and that the interaction is equivalent to a rotating cantilever governed by torque balance. Force amplitude is determined by stem stiffness and geometry, while the timescale is set by circumnutation rate. Twining occurs only after reaching a critical torque threshold, corresponding to a deformation that reflects support stability and geometric reach. Motorized perturbations further show that twining time scales inversely with effective circumnutation rate. Together, these results show how self-generated motion extracts actionable information about the environment, while the tapered geometry and spatially varying mechanics of the shoot encode the decision-making threshold for attachment.

title: Data-driven traction force microscopy in 3D collagen hydrogels
abstract: Three-dimensional traction force microscopy (3DTFM) in fibrillar hydrogels typically models the extracellular matrix as a continuum. We present data-driven 3DTFM (DD-TFM), which reconstructs fiber networks from confocal images and models them as discrete fiber networks mechanically calibrated by shear rheology. We validate DD-TFM in silico and apply it to endothelial cells, quantifying cell-generated forces and matrix stresses at the fiber level. Compared with continuum TFM DD-TFM reveals network-guided matrix deformations, shifting 3DTFM toward fiber-resolved force calculation.

title: Torque-optimized body morphing enables rapid surface to underwater diving in whirligig beetles
abstract: Known for their rapid water surface locomotion, whirligig beetles (Gyrinidae) are also fast divers. They can transition from the surface to underwater swimming in under 100 ms. Diving requires them to generate sufficient hydrodynamic torque to break the water surface and reorient the body. However, the mechanism by which whirligigs create the necessary pitch-down torque is unknown. Here, we show that their diving is achieved by bending the abdomen. The inertial hydrodynamic pressure on the flexed abdomen generates the torque necessary for surface breaking and body rotation. The torque is maximized at an abdominal angle of 45{degrees}, whereas for effective diving, whirligigs display a preferential abdominal angle of around 28{degrees}, closely aligning with the angle that maximizes the torque-to-drag ratio. This abdominal angle is optimized by balancing torque generation with the drag penalty. Our findings inspire a mechanism for surface-to-underwater transition, offering design principles for multimodal robots capable of locomotion across the air-water interface.

title: L-type channel voltage-dependent facilitation results from asymmetric π-H and π-π quadrangle interactions at DI-DII domains
abstract: Voltage-dependent facilitation (VDF) is a distinctive phenomenon of L-type voltage-gated calcium (CaV) channels, in which depolarized prepulse voltages increase inward current by up to several fold. Despite extensive study, the molecular origin and biophysical mechanisms underlying the L-type channel (CaV1.1-CaV1.4) VDF remain elusive. A serendipitous observation that solutions stored in polypropylene tubes eliminated CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 L-type channel VDF led us to identify the leachable 2,4-di-tert-butylphenol (2,4-DTBP) as a selective VDF inhibitor. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations revealed previously unreported asymmetric {pi}-H and {pi}-{pi} interdomain quadrangle interactions at the DI-DII pore-domain (PD) interface in L-type channels. Disruption of these quadrangle interactions in CaV1.2 via point mutagenesis abolished the VDF. Whereas, introducing the quadrangle interaction onto non-VDF-displaying CaV<2.1 channels induced robust VDF. This work provides the first molecular evidence for the VDF endpoint: L-type channel-specific interdomain quadrangle interactions asymmetrically positioned at the DI-DII PD interface.

title: How the Azadithiolate Ligand Impacts O2-Stability of Group B -Hydrogenase ToHydA
abstract: [FeFe]-hydrogenases are metalloenzymes that catalyze the reversible oxidation and production of H2, making them potential candidates for sustainable energy solutions. However, their practical application is restricted by their extreme O2 sensitivity, which leads to irreversible active site degradation. A newly characterized Group B hydrogenase, ToHydA from Thermosediminibacter oceani, has exhibited exceptional O2-stability even after longtime exposure to air. In ToHydA, the highly conserved proton-transporting cysteine (C212) safeguards the H-cluster from O2-induced degradation by formation of the Hinact state. In this study, we investigate the effects of replacing the azadithiolate (ADT) ligand of [2Fe]H with propanedithiolate (PDT), revealing that this substitution prevents the formation of the Hinact and Htrans states observed in ToHydA WT (bearing the ADT ligand). By combining ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we show that a favorable interaction between the nitrogen bridgehead of the ADT ligand and the C212 sidechain is crucial for stabilizing these states. The absence of this interaction in ToHydAPDT (bearing the PDT ligand) prevents the C212 sidechain from approaching the Fed center of [2Fe]H, thereby reducing Hinact accumulation. Moreover, as-isolated ToHydAPDT predominantly exhibits the Hhyd state, which is unusual for [FeFe]-hydrogenases with bound PDT ligand. These findings demonstrate how ligand substitution at the [2Fe]H site of ToHydA affects the structural dynamics, offering detailed molecular insights into the ligand-dependent modulation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases.

title: Two cortical mechanisms for natural audiovisual processing
abstract: Understanding how the human brain processes natural audiovisual information remains a central challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Progress has been limited by the difficulty of modeling complex audiovisual stimuli; prior work has therefore relied largely on short, controlled, or unimodal stimuli, leaving cortical mechanisms supporting real-world comprehension poorly characterized. Although recent AI advances enable extraction of high-dimensional, time-resolved features from naturalistic stimuli, how cortical regions dynamically prioritize auditory and visual information as time unfolds remains largely unexplored. Using large-scale fMRI data collected during movie viewing, we developed two complementary prediction-based approaches to map moment-by-moment sensory processing across cortex: one detects sustained periods when one modality predicts a region better than the other, identifying regions that switch the modality they encode for meaningful stretches of time; while the other identifies periods when both modalities predict the region well, revealing balanced audiovisual representations. Together, these analyses reveal two cortical patterns of audiovisual processing: two modality-switching ``bows" (a posterior bow encircling category-selective visual cortex and an anterior bow spanning dorsolateral frontal cortex) and an arrow-like axis jointly representing both modalities (extending from lateral occipital into temporal cortex). We further show that switching is not driven by reduced low-level information in the non-dominant modality, but by reduced cortical encoding of that information, suggesting active sensory reweighting. Modality dominance also cannot be explained simply by the dominant modality conveying a region's preferred concepts; switching regions do not merely track whichever modality expresses these concepts.Together, these systems suggest a cortical architecture that adaptively reweights sensory inputs while maintaining balanced multimodal representations during naturalistic comprehension.

title: Direct CDK1 engagement underlies carbaryl-induced genotoxic cell cycle arrest
abstract: Carbaryl, a widely used carbamate pesticide, has been epidemiologically associated with genotoxic and carcinogenic outcomes in exposed human populations, including elevated cancer risk at several tissue sites and, in some agricultural communities, chronic tubulointerstitial kidney disease of unknown etiology (CKDu). However, the cellular mechanisms underlying these associations, and whether carbaryl acts uniformly across tissues, remain poorly defined. Screening a panel of cell lines of distinct species and lineage, we found that carbaryl elicits pronounced, dose-dependent cytotoxicity and cell cycle arrest selectively in a renal tubular epithelial line (IMCD3) and, to a lesser extent, a cervical epithelial line (HeLa), while a fibroblast line (NIH3T3) was unaffected. In IMCD3 cells, carbaryl induces S- and G2/M-phase arrest through direct binding to DNA and consequent DNA damage, triggers Bcl-2-mediated late apoptosis independently of reactive oxygen species, and drives irreversible mitotic arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations, cellular thermal shift assays, and kinase measurements converge on CDK1 as a direct target of carbaryl: carbaryl destabilises the CDK1 active site and inhibits its catalytic activity, whereas CDK2 is engaged through an opposing, rigidifying mode with no functional consequence. This asymmetry provides a coherent mechanistic basis for the combined S-phase and G2/M arrest observed. Together, these findings establish carbaryl as a genotoxic, cell-cycle-disrupting agent with tissue-selective potency acting directly on CDK1, and provide a cell-based mechanistic framework for interpreting its reported associations with renal and other tissue pathologies in exposed human populations.

title: Initiation codon context governs translation-coupled mRNA decay and coordinated expression in the human parasite Leishmania
abstract: In the absence of canonical, promoter-based transcriptional regulation, Leishmania has evolved alternative regulatory mechanisms for adaptive gene expression, including post-transcriptional control via differential mRNA turnover. While this mechanism is recognized as critical in Leishmania, fundamental aspects of transcript stability in these parasites remain to be elucidated, such as the role of translation initiation-mediated mRNA decay. We addressed this important gap by investigating the role of the initiation codon context (Kozak sequence) in gene expression in L. donovani. Mapping Kozak sequences across the trypanosomatid genomes revealed important differences in nucleotide preference across the genus and sub-genus levels, suggesting important cis-regulatory function. Within a single species, only a small subset of possible Kozak sequences is associated with several start codons, further supporting their role in expression control. Transgenic L. donovani lines expressing EGFP under the control of distinct Kozak variants indeed demonstrated that the nucleotide context of the start codon directly modulates both protein expression and mRNA stability, which was associated with increased recruitment of mRNA to heavy polysomes. Parasite exposure to the translation inhibitor cycloheximide restored EGFP expression driven by a weak Kozak sequence, revealing a direct link between mRNA stability and Kozak-mediated translatability. RNA-seq analysis of parasites arrested for transcription or translation elongation revealed transcripts enriched for the GO terms RNA modification and pseudouridine synthesis as key targets for translation-dependent mRNA turnover. The segregation of these transcripts into functional clusters with distinct Kozak profiles further suggests that Kozak sequence composition defines Kozak-governed regulons in Leishmania. Within this regulatory framework, the -3 nucleotide is identified as the key positional determinant driving differential transcript abundance. Our work uncovers a key role for translation initiation-coupled mRNA decay in Leishmania gene expression regulation adding a previously underappreciated layer of post-transcriptional regulation in parasite adaptation.

title: A Large Yield Model for Crop Production and Design in Western Canada
abstract: With a changing climate, disease pressure, and other production threats, it is critical to ensure that crop producers are well-positioned to protect and optimize yields. In this work we present LYM-1, the first large-scale, multi-crop model for the prediction of yield performance in the Canadian prairies. This is enabled by a large dataset containing over 4.7 million yield observations across 10 different crop types, distributed over 23 growing years. Leveraging additional data sources for weather and soil properties allows the model to reason about the complex interactions between genetics, environment, and management which underlie yield. The trained model is not only effective at predicting the yield for held-out data, but also reveals scientifically and agronomically relevant effects such as the interaction between solar radiation and nitrogen uptake. We show that the architecture and training approach used in LYM-1 allows it to perform inference given incomplete queries where some model inputs are unspecified, while also establishing an advantage over popular linear and machine learning models in predictive performance.

title: Biotin-operated ligand trapping enables dynamic spatial redistribution of protein and organelle in living cells
abstract: Controlling protein localization through chemical biology tools is essential for mechanistic interrogations, functional perturbations, and therapeutic development. While existing tools cover a wide range of applications, no single approach simultaneously enables inducible trapping, controlled release, and visualization of a protein of interest (POI). To address this gap, we developed Biotin-Operated Ligand Trapping (BOLT), which combines a HaloTag-fused POI with a streptavidin trap. Desthiobiotin-conjugated Janelia Fluor HaloTag ligands enable POI visualization, trapping, and biotin-operated release. We demonstrate BOLT's capacity in synchronized secretory cargo release, microtubule-directed organelle movement and hitchhiking, and ectopically localizing nuclear transcription factor. Importantly, pulse-chase BOLT further reveals bidirectional endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi trafficking of an endogenous Golgi enzyme and distinguishes recycled from newly synthesized enzyme populations using distinct HTLs. Altogether, BOLT provides an all-in-one platform to interrogate how subcellular localization regulates protein function across HaloTag-compatible systems.

title: Synaptic density imaging associates with performance but not self-report in autism
abstract: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental condition with considerable between-person variability and unknown biological etiology. Diagnosis of autism in adults relies on measurement of performance (e.g., clinician rating of social behavior, standardized assessment of cognition) and self-report of autism features. Our prior work revealed a strong relationship between clinician ratings of social function in autism and in vivo measures of synaptic density as measured by [11C]UCB-J PET (Matuskey et al., 2025). However, it is not understood how the measured aspects of the autism phenotype index underlying biology. Here, in a sample of 12 autistic adults, we address this question by relating synaptic density imaging to a range of performance measures, such as cognition and face recognition, in contrast to self-report measures. Our results identify a dissociation between these measurement types in that synaptic density correlates strongly with measures of performance but shows virtually no relationship with self-report. These findings suggest that, while self-report and performance measures share variance in characterizing phenotypes in autism, they diverge when mapping onto the underlying biology. Results suggest that higher synaptic density may index a general mechanism that facilitates social and cognitive performance across a range of tasks. These data also indicate that performance and self-report measures are not interchangeable in capturing brain-behavior correspondences in autism, a finding that can guide measure selection in future biomarker studies and clinical research.

title: Thalamic Dysconnectivity and Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Background and Hypothesis Negative symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) are associated with poor functional outcomes and reduced quality of life; however, effective treatments remain limited. A better understanding of the underlying brain mechanisms is needed to develop better treatments. Neuroimaging studies implicate multiple brain networks in negative symptoms, though findings remain heterogeneous, potentially reflecting the multidimensionality of both symptoms and brain networks. Larger, more systematic dissections are required to identify the key hub(s) underlying negative symptoms. Study Design Structural MRI data from 394 participants (210 SSD, 184 healthy controls [HC]) were analyzed to identify cortical thickness and subcortical volume demonstrating both SSD-HC differences and associations with negative symptoms measured by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS). Regions meeting both criteria were selected as seeds for resting-state functional connectivity analyses in 143 SSD patients to examine association with negative symptoms and their subdomains. Study Results The thalamus was the only region demonstrating significant structural abnormalities both in SSD and an association with BNSS total score (p-FDR<0.05). Functional-network-defined thalamic subregions were subsequently examined. Several thalamic hypoconnectivities were significantly corresponded with negative symptoms, involving thalamic subregions associated with the cortical default mode, somatosensory, medial temporal, and dorsal attention networks (p=0.001, corrected<0.05). Blunted affect showed the most extensive thalamic connectivity alterations, involving the striatum, cerebellum, and temporoparietal junction/superior temporal sulcus (TPJ-STS). Thalamic hypoconnectivity with TPJ-STS was also associated with overall negative symptoms and anhedonia. Conclusions This study identifies the thalamus as a central hub of negative symptom-related dysfunction in SSD and highlights specific thalamic subnetworks as potential targets for circuit-based interventions.

title: Clustered and diffuse sensory corticostriatal wirings define complementary interneuron circuits
abstract: In the striatum, interneurons tightly control the activity of output neurons, the striatal projection neurons (SPN). Among these striatal interneurons, parvalbumin-expressing (PV) and somatostatin-expressing (SOM) cells exhibit markedly distinct electrophysiological and anatomical properties, suggesting differential integration into striatal circuits and distinct forms of feedforward inhibition onto SPN. However, it remains unclear whether differences already emerge at the level of corticostriatal connectivity and if they shape specific interactions with cortical inputs to SPN. Here, we investigated the spatial organization of the projections from the primary and secondary somatosensory areas (S1 and S2), onto striatal PV and SOM interneurons and SPN. With a combination of anatomical tracing and functional circuit mapping, we characterized key features of corticostriatal connectivity, including input number, origin, spacing, overlap and strength. We found that input spacing and strength, at both the individual cell and population levels, were the principal features distinguishing PV and SOM interneurons. In contrast, connectivity differed primarily in input number and laminar organization across S1 and S2. Our findings suggest two potential modes of interaction between interneurons and SPN connectivity: one in which PV interneurons receive S1 inputs structured in large clusters, that densely overlap with those of neighboring SPN, providing an anatomical substrate for potential neuronal assemblies. And another in which SOM interneurons also receive abundant cortical inputs, but thinly disseminated across S1 and S2 and that overlap little with those of SPN, potentially shaping these cell integration through input cross-interaction. These cell-type principles of corticostriatal wiring may support distinct forms of striatal computation.

title: Learning source weights for target-position estimation: comparing fixed weights and an input-dependent rule
abstract: Estimating an object's location requires combining uncertain measurements. Weights derived from an earlier calibration may become inappropriate when measurement errors change. We examined whether learning from noisy reference measurements improves position estimates, and whether weights computed from current inputs improve further than one learned set of weights used throughout evaluation. In simulations, we generated noisy position measurements of a target that remained fixed within each trial. Each two-input method combined the current measurement with the mean of three initial measurements. Measurement-accuracy reductions and added measurement offsets applied only after initialization. The estimator received no current or previous true target position. We repeated coordinate calibration, training, validation, and independent evaluation 100 times in each of four error conditions. Recalibration and fixed-weight learning explained most of the improvement over earlier supplied weights under reduced measurement accuracy and temporal correlation. With occasional large measurement errors, input-dependent weighting reduced mean squared error by 4.05% relative to learned fixed weights and assigned lower mean weights to measurements with added offsets. Its additional benefit was below 0.5% under independent errors and reduced current accuracy, while fixed weights had slightly lower mean error under temporal correlation. Methods using longer observation histories performed better in several conditions. Sensitivity analysis showed that shared coordinate bias and correlated reference errors limit conclusions about physical accuracy. The results show benefits and limits of recalibration, input-dependent weighting, and observation history within these measurement models.

title: SroA links SigS-dependent stress signaling to metabolic remodeling in Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus encounters diverse environmental conditions during colonization and infection, including fluctuations in nutrient availability, oxidative stress, and oxygen limitation. Adaptation to these environments requires regulatory systems that coordinate stress responses with metabolic physiology. The extracytoplasmic function sigma factor SigS contributes to stress adaptation and virulence in S. aureus and directly activates expression of the sroAB operon, which encodes the small proteins SroA and SroB. Previous work demonstrated that SroA participates in feedback regulation of sigS expression, but the broader physiological role of SroA has remained unclear. To further define the regulatory functions of SroA, we performed RNA sequencing following inducible overexpression of sroA in S. aureus. Transcriptome analysis identified altered expression of genes associated with nitrate respiration, nucleotide biosynthesis, stress responses, and nutrient acquisition. Northern blot and quantitative RT-PCR analysis confirmed repression of narG and narJ transcripts following SroA overexpression. Consistent with these transcriptional changes, SroA overexpression impaired nitrate reduction and produced a modest but significant growth disadvantage under anaerobic conditions in chemically defined medium supplemented with glucose and nitrate. In addition to repression of nitrate respiration genes, SroA overexpression reduced expression of genes involved in de novo purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis, while transcripts associated with stress responses and nutrient acquisition, including sosA and pstS, were increased. Together, these findings support a role for SroA in modulating nitrate respiration-associated pathways and growth under conditions supporting anaerobic respiration, linking SigS-dependent stress signaling to metabolic adaptation in S. aureus.

title: Lactate epigenetically shapes tumor cell states in H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas
abstract: H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are lethal and lack treatment options. These tumors exhibit tumor heterogeneity with aggressive oligodendrocyte precursor (OPC)- and mesenchymal (MES)-like cell states. Because all tumor cells bear H3K27M, tumor heterogeneity has been attributed to microenvironmental cues that remain obscure. H3K27M DMGs exhibit increased glycolysis and the Warburg effect to produce lactate. Lactate can directly modify histone lysines including H3K27Lac, and we hypothesized that lactate epigenetically regulates tumor cell states in H3K27M DMGs. We undertook a comprehensive and integrated analysis of H3K27M DMG cell lines, animal models, tumor tissues, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy in patients to decipher the epigenetic roles of lactate. Here, we report that H3K27M cells uniquely exhibit elevation of the activating mark H3K27Lac. We observed significant heterogeneity in lactate levels within tumors, and the addition of exogenous lactate resulted in marked increases in H3K27Lac and the expression of critical OPC- and MES- like gene signature genes, which correlates with poorer patient outcomes. Our therapeutic approach leverages the inhibition of CBP/p300, which deposits both H3K27Lac and H3K27ac. Targeting CBP/p300 effectively reduces both H3K27Lac and H3K27ac levels, suppresses key OPC- and MES-like signatures, and shows efficacy in preclinical models. Collectively, our findings identify lactate as a key player in the epigenetic regulation of tumor cell state heterogeneity and suggest that targeting this pathway offers promise for addressing the heterogeneous complexities of H3K27M DMGs.

title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

title: Metatranscriptomic Identification of Co- and Incidental Infections in Marine Turtles Reveals Complex Disease Aetiologies
abstract: Traditional veterinary pathology investigations on wild animals generally conclude a primary cause of death based on a combination of observed clinical signs, gross and microscopic lesions, microbial culture and PCR. However, these methods may fail to capture the broader microbial community of the host. We employed metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the potential pathobiome of necropsied marine turtles, comparing these findings with corresponding veterinary pathology reports. Tissue samples were collected from 76 individuals spanning three species of marine turtles -- the green turtle (Chelonia mydas), the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), and the loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) -- across the coastline of New South Wales, Australia. Reported causes of mortality ranged from infectious disease to trauma. We identified a diverse range of parasites within the genera Neospirochis, Hapalotrema, Paraorgymatobothrium, Eimeria and Callitetrarhynchus, and bacteria including the genera Aeromonas, Clostridium, and Vibrio. Novel viruses of the families Astroviridae, Caliciviridae, Hepaciviridae, Hepeviridae, Nyamivirdae, Orthomyxoviridae, Picobirnaviridae and Rhabdoviridae were also identified. In cases where infectious disease was noted in the pathology report, we frequently observed high pathogen read counts consistent with the listed primary diagnoses. However, we also detected a range of incidental infections involving eukaryotic parasites, bacteria, and viruses. The diversity of infectious agents detected in marine turtles suggests that the observed disease outcomes are unlikely to be driven by a single causative agent, but rather by complex interactions between host health, the pathobiome, and environmental stressors. We discuss the potential implications for turtle health and conservation.

title: Patronin condensation integrates recognition, protection and organization of microtubule minus ends
abstract: Microtubule minus ends are central to non-centrosomal microtubule organization, yet how their recognition, protection and molecular organization are integrated remains unclear. Here we show that Drosophila Patronin forms dynamic condensates at microtubule minus ends through a prion-like domain (PrLD). PrLD-mediated condensation cooperates with the CKK domain and a second CKK-independent recognition region to convert weak or broadly distributed microtubule-binding activities into persistent minus-end recognition and tracking. Replacing the PrLD with a heterologous phase-separating HNRNPA1 IDR restores minus-end targeting, indicating that condensation capacity rather than PrLD primary sequence is critical. Patronin condensates further form a protective cap that resists minus-end depolymerization and recruit the cytoskeletal regulators Sas-4, Katanin and Ena. Disrupting PrLD multivalency impairs Patronin localization at multiple developmental sites and causes early organismal lethality. Thus, Patronin condensation creates a physiologically essential microtubule minus-end compartment coupling end recognition, stabilization and cytoskeletal organization.

title: A dsRNA Virus Converts Early Endosomes into Stable Replication Organelles Through Maturation Arrest and Retrograde Transport
abstract: Infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) and infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (IPNV) are major animal pathogens that impose a heavy burden on the poultry and aquaculture industries. Yet, major aspects of their unique replication program remain unknown. IBDV is unusual among double-stranded RNA viruses in that it replicates in association with host endosomes. We previously demonstrated this association to be orchestrated by the viral protein VP3 and the early endosomal lipid phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PtdIns(3)P], suggesting an essential role for VP3 in forming birnaviruses specialized replication compartments. Here, combining high-resolution fluorescence and correlative light-electron microscopy with diverse molecular and biochemical analyses, we define how the IBDV protein VP3 targets and remodels host endosomes, and establish that endosome-associated replication is conserved in members of the Birnaviridae family. We show that IBDV VP3 targets early endosomes via the PtdIns(3)P effector Early Endosomal Antigen 1 (EEA1) to arrest their maturation and prompt their association with the Golgi complex via ESCPE-1-mediated retrograde transport. We further show that IPNV also exploits endosomal membranes for replication in a PtdIns(3)P dependent manner, although for this virus VP3 engages endosomes through an EEA1-independent mechanism yet to be determined. This work uncovers how birnaviruses exploit a single viral protein to orchestrate endosome remodeling and intracellular trafficking to establish specialized replication compartments while revealing both conserved and host-adapted features of birnaviruses replication.

title: ESX-1 remodels the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen storage compartment in macrophages
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) secretes antigenic proteins that drive protective T cell responses, yet how Mtb intracellular localization affects the trafficking and spatiotemporal distribution of mycobacterial antigens in macrophages remains elusive. Here, we developed a split fluorescent protein reporter to monitor the dynamics of the TB vaccine lead antigen Ag85B in infected human macrophages. We discovered that Mtb triggers the formation and remodeling of two distinct types of Mtb Antigen Storage Compartment (MASC) that retains Ag85 within macrophage membranes. Using subcellular spatial proteomics, we profiled the composition of the MASC, identifying both the Mtb and macrophage proteins that constitute these compartments. Unexpectedly, MASCs are defined by metabolic compartmentalization and rewiring to lipid metabolism in both the macrophage and Mtb. Thus, Mtb builds via the ESX-1 system a metabolically distinct antigen storage compartment in immune cells, with potential implications for antigen selection and delivery in TB vaccine development.

title: Disentangling maternal pregnancy and fetal-specific plasma signatures through integrated proteomics and site-specific N-glycoproteomics
abstract: During pregnancy, mother and fetus co-exist albeit as two physiologically distinct individuals, connected through the placenta and the umbilical cord. This connection allows for the exchange of vital substances, while individual blood homeostasis remains intact. We hypothesized that comparing maternal and cord plasma (N-glyco)proteomes would provide insights into the biological communication and unique physiological state of each individual. As comparing only matched maternal and umbilical cord blood plasma misses a crucial identifier in determining whether observed changes are related to infancy, pregnancy or both, we designed a triad study by adding a non-pregnant women control group. This allowed us to distinguish pregnancy-specific proteins and their potentially altered N-glycosylation from those in infancy. We found that the fetus and mother have distinct proteomes, N-glycoproteoforms and alternative complement regulation. Moreover, we observed that pregnancy in women led to specific N-glycosylation changes on a select set of primarily HDL-associated and acute-phase proteins. Lastly, our data provide evidence for an early fetal development of the humoral immune system as especially fetal IgM displayed distinctive N-glycosylation signatures.

title: Environmental correlates of understory plant diversity and distribution in a temperate climate-change refugium
abstract: Aim Regional climate-change refugia - areas where abiotic conditions related to hydrology and topography sustain unique plant communities despite an otherwise unsuitable regional macroclimate - have been essential for maintaining biodiversity through past climatic transitions. At fine spatial scales, regional refugia can also contain microrefugia, where canopy structure and topography strongly buffer understory microclimate. We tested whether such microrefugia structure understory plant communities within a regional climate-change refugium, where sheltered, groundwater-fed canyons have sustained a biogeographically distinctive flora since the Last Glacial Maximum. Location Temperate forest in the North American Great Plains, Nebraska, USA. Methods In a 20.2-ha forest inventory plot spanning a sharp topographic gradient, we quantified diversity, composition, and distributions and of understory woody and herbaceous plants across seven functional groups along fine-scale topographic, light, and soil moisture gradients. Results Woody species density and richness were significantly higher within sheltered microrefugia in canyon bottoms and on forested slopes and strongly decreased with increasing canopy openness, whereas C4 grass richness was highest along the exposed, high-light forest-prairie ecotone, reflecting divergent functional group responses to microclimate buffering. Soil moisture structured richness across functional groups: woody plant and C3 grass richness peaked at moisture extremes, sedge richness at intermediate moisture variability, and C4 grass richness declined with increasing moisture variability. Both woody and herbaceous understory plants showed strong variation in composition with topography; in particular, woody seedlings and graminoids exhibited strong species turnover with increasing elevation. Main Conclusions These results demonstrate that topographically driven microrefugia support disproportionate understory biodiversity and suggest that protecting both regional refugia and finer-scale microrefugia will be critical for conserving plant communities, including species documented exclusively in microrefugia, as macroclimate continues to change.

title: STEM-LM: Spatio-Temporal Ecological Modeling via Masked Language Model for Multi-Species Distribution
abstract: Species distribution models (SDMs) are central to biodiversity forecasting and conservation decision-making. As ecological datasets grow in size, dimensionality, and resolution, there is a need for flexible yet scalable SDMs tailored to large-scale species observation data. Inspired by the masked modeling approach in natural language processing and genomics, if we treat each species' presence or absence as a token, and a site's species assemblage together with its spatio-temporal and ecological covariates as analogous to a sentence, we can learn joint co-occurrence structure by reconstructing masked species from their neighboring sites. We propose STEM-LM, a Transformer-based SDM that applies masked language modeling to multi-species distribution modeling with explicit consideration of spatio-temporal structure. By applying dynamic masking rates during training, a single trained model can support both purely spatio-temporal/ecological prediction and prediction conditioned on arbitrary subsets of observed species. On a North American butterfly dataset, a Northeast US demersal fish trawl survey, and a global plant distribution dataset, STEM-LM has the highest discrimination (AUROC) among all compared methods, and its rank-monotonicity (continuous Boyce index) is either the best or close to the best.

title: Abundance redistribution increases predator-prey interaction potentials among North American birds
abstract: Species are dramatically shifting their geographical ranges, yet the consequences of these spatial redistributions on species interactions have not been examined at broad spatial and temporal scales. Here, we investigate how the redistribution of species abundance over the past 50 years affects the potential for predator-prey interactions among North American birds. We first predict potential predator-prey interactions based on existing data and functional traits, then construct a novel, abundance-weighted metric of interaction potential for each pair of predator and prey in local communities. Across North America, the potential for predator-prey interactions has been increasing over time. We further show that this widespread increasing trend in interaction potentials is mostly driven by higher abundances of predator species. The spatial redistributions of predators and prey lead to turnover of interactions within local communities, and the turnover is less associated with changes in climate but more associated with human-induced land use changes. title: Categorical rhythmic patterns do not predict song preference in zebra finches
abstract: Categorical rhythmic patterns are fundamental features found in language and music across cultures. In humans, these rhythmic patterns occur in both vocal production and perceptual preference, highlighting a link between rhythmic production and preference. Categorical rhythmic patterns have recently been identified in animal vocalisations too, but whether rhythm production is linked with rhythmic preferences in non-human animals remains unclear. Within this context, zebra finches (Taeniopygia castanotis) are of particular interest, as both sexes develop a song preference, and their song has been suggested to exhibit an isochronous temporal structure. Here, we tested for the first time whether zebra finches prefer songs containing discrete rhythmic patterns, using operant preference tests with either two or four rhythmic patterns. Our results show that no categorical rhythmic pattern was consistently preferred across the population, although responses varied among individuals. These findings indicate that categorical rhythmic patterns are unlikely to be a primary driver of song preference in zebra finches. Together with previous work in other vocal-learning birds, our results suggest that preferences for categorical rhythmic patterns may not be universal and could instead reflect species-specific features of vocal displays rather than the rhythmic categories characteristic of human music.

title: "Mine" or "yours"? Acoustic structure of food calls predicts sharing decisions in marmosets
abstract: Foraging and feeding are often associated with vocalisations across animal species. Food calls may function to claim ownership of resources or recruit others to feeding sites, yet their potential role in facilitating food sharing remains poorly understood. This study investigates the relationship between food calls and food-sharing behaviour in common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), focusing on adult-infant interactions, where food transfers are most frequent. We analysed over 1000 food interactions across six groups, categorising events as non-sharing (without begging or despite begging) or sharing (proactive, resisted, or facilitated). We examined the spectro-temporal structure of food calls produced immediately before each interaction. Food transfers were more likely to occur when preceded by a food call, suggesting a functional link between food calls and sharing. Random forest models reliably classified food calls according to interaction type, while generalized linear mixed models identified acoustic variation associated with sharing outcomes. Our results suggest that food calls encode information to either encourage or deter conspecific (infant) approach, influencing food transfer outcomes. These findings highlight the role of food calls in modulating social interactions around food in marmosets, advancing our understanding of vocal communication and its integration with cooperative behaviours in primates.

title: A look inside the net: freshwater turtles assort with conspecifics in feeding aggregations
abstract: Historically, non-avian reptiles were assumed to be non-social - yet recent studies show diverse social behaviours in squamates, crocodilians, and turtles. Here, we investigate social structure within feeding aggregations of three freshwater turtle species caught in baited traps in a coastal marsh over 12 years. In 488 instances in which traps contained turtles, 45% contained multiple individuals, and these aggregations were strongly positively assorted by species. Midland painted turtles (Chrysemys picta marginata) and Blanding's turtles (Emydoidea blandingii) were captured with conspecifics more often than expected in non-social null models. Snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina), the largest species in this study, were captured with conspecifics at a frequency similar to that predicted by null models, and were avoided by heterospecifics. This suggests that species differences play a role in how feeding aggregations are structured, with painted and Blanding's turtles driving strong positive species assortment while avoiding snapping turtles around food sources. We did not detect significant intraspecific sex assortment in any of the three species, nor did turtle body size strongly affect the probability of aggregating with conspecifics at the perceived food source in the traps. Our study illustrates how long-term monitoring data can be used to investigate social structure in wild populations, an approach that may be valuable for species of conservation concern.

title: Ambient-Condition Visualization of Metalloenzyme Reactive Intermediates Enabled by the SHINERS Paradigm
abstract: Reactive metal-oxygen intermediates are central to metalloenzyme catalysis, yet their low populations and short lifetimes make vibrational characterization under aqueous reaction conditions challenging. Here, we establish shell-isolated nanoparticle-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SHINERS) as a powerful vibrational approach for visualizing reaction-associated metal-ligand signatures of reactive metalloenzyme states. Across the heme and non-heme iron enzymes TauD, VioC, CYP119, and TqaLNc, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational information on reactive coordination states. In TauD and VioC, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational characterization of Fe(IV)=O intermediates. In CYP119, an isotope-sensitive Fe(IV)=O vibration is assigned to P450 Compound I generated by m-CPBA, including under lauric-acid turnover conditions. Most notably, in TqaLNc, combined 18O- and 15N-sensitive vibrational responses support formation of the proposed (R)HN-Fe(IV)=O coordination state and the dynamic-coordination mechanism underlying selective C-N bond formation. These results demonstrate that SHINERS can serve as a powerful technique for the in situ vibrational visualization of reactive intermediates and their coordination states in metalloenzyme catalysis.

title: Circular Data Analysis for Spatial Omics
abstract: Many biological quantities in omics are inherently periodic or directional, including circadian phase, cell-cycle position, and cellular orientation. Treating such quantities as ordinary linear variables can introduce artificial discontinuities and obscure biological interpretation. Circular methods are well developed across directional statistics, bioinformatics, and spatial statistics, but practical guidance for omics applications remains limited. We present key considerations for circular data analysis in single-cell and spatial omics, including the provenance and observational unit of the circular quantity, the inferential or predictive objective, the distinction between tissue composition and residual spatial dependence, and the choice of appropriate models. We describe relevant approaches for circular representation, inference, clustering, regression, machine learning, and spatial analysis, together with representative R software. Their practical use is illustrated through spatial transcriptomic case studies of derived circadian peak phase in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease and latent cell-cycle position in human ovarian cancer. These examples demonstrate how the definition of the angle, its observational unit, and tissue heterogeneity shape appropriate analysis and interpretation, including when spatial modeling is not warranted. We conclude with practical recommendations and directions for future methodological development.

title: Complex folding kinetics of multi-domain proteins disentangled with periodic forces by magnetic tweezers
abstract: Force spectroscopy enables direct investigation of the interplay between free energy and transition kinetics in proteins and nucleic acids. However, multi-domain proteins often display multiple intermediate structures with diverse stabilities and kinetics, making equilibrium conditions difficult to achieve and out-of-equilibrium experiments challenging to interpret. We introduce a single-molecule force spectroscopy assay using periodic forces and high-resolution magnetic tweezers to bridge different stabilities, selectively enhance intermediate populations, and rigorously analyze multi-domain protein folding kinetics at quasi-equilibrium. By applying well-defined periodic square force functions with tunable steady states, we first validate our framework on the two-state folder {lambda}6-85, demonstrating that periodic force experiments can reproduce equilibrium kinetics. Extending this approach to the multi-domain protein mimic (Protein L), we show that tuning force, frequency, and amplitude enhances populations of distinct intermediate states. Finally, we dissect the entangled states of the hybrid two-domain protein {lambda}-L, where a 100-fold difference in domain kinetics precludes equilibrium analysis, by expanding from a two-state to a three-state periodic force protocol to direct intermediate populations. Our assay and analysis framework open new possibilities for deciphering complex multi-domain folds and their multi-dimensional folding pathways.

title: Pathogenic DRP1 variants reveal a role for biomolecular condensation in mitochondrial fission
abstract: Fission is essential for proper mitochondrial function and for cellular homeostasis. Dysfunction in mitochondrial fission is associated with several neurological disorders, including the rare and lethal encephalopathy EMPF1, which is caused by de novo heterozygous DNM1L variants. DNM1L encodes the mitochondrial fission mechanoenzyme DRP1, which can intrinsically self-assemble and induce membrane scission. Wild-type DRP1 puncta that appear throughout the cytoplasm are thought to be pre-scission complexes of well-ordered oligomeric assemblies. Immunofluorescence imaging of patient-derived EMPF1 fibroblasts carrying assembly-deficient DNM1L variants reveals elongated mitochondrial networks consistent with impaired fission. Despite this loss-of-function phenotype, these cells retain essentially wild-type numbers of DRP1 puncta. We confirmed the previously reported inability of purified pathogenic DRP1 variants p.Gly363Asp and p.Gly401Ser to assemble under conditions in which WT DRP1 forms helical polymers. Under macromolecular crowding conditions, however, both wild-type and mutant DRP1 access condensed states whose formation depends on protein concentration and solution conditions. Acute treatment of EMPF1 fibroblasts with 1,6-hexanediol preferentially alters DRP1 puncta fluorescence intensity and distribution in mutant cells relative to wild type, indicating genotype-dependent differences in puncta material properties. Together, these findings support a model in which DRP1 puncta occupy a continuum of condensed states, only a subset of which mature into fission-competent assemblies, revealing biomolecular condensation as a previously unrecognized layer of DRP1 regulation. Biasing DRP1 along this continuum may provide a mechanistic basis for impaired fission in EMPF1 and suggest opportunities to restore productive assembly in select pathogenic contexts.

title: Discovering Latent Scientific Concepts through Discrete Representation Learning
abstract: Scientific imaging is undergoing a fundamental transformation. Advances in multiplex immunofluorescence, computational pathology, and electron microscopy now enable observation of biological and physical systems at unprecedented spatial resolution. Rather than simply classifying known objects, these data offer the opportunity to discover previously unknown organizational principles. However, scientific image datasets are typically highly curated, information-rich, and limited in size, making reliable representation learning particularly challenging. We show that standard continuous self-supervised adaptation can become unstable in this regime, allowing teacher representations to drift and degrading downstream transfer. We introduce Kodiak, a discrete representation learning architecture that discovers latent scientific concepts through Sinkhorn-balanced codebook assignments. Instead of learning unconstrained continuous embeddings, Kodiak constructs a reusable vocabulary of discrete concepts that provides stable supervision for both masked-patch prediction and cross-view representation learning within a single-stage framework. Across five scientific imaging domains, including multiplex immunofluorescence for pancreatic cancer pathology and scanning electron microscopy, Kodiak consistently improves representation quality under both continued foundation-model adaptation and training from scratch. Beyond improved classification and transfer,the learned concepts are interpretable, reusable, and produce spatially coherent concept maps that support applications such as cell phenotyping, segmentation-free patch phenotyping, spatial niche discovery, tissue organization, and materials characterization. We view Kodiak as the representation-learning engine of our foundation model for spatial biology. More broadly, our results suggest that discrete representation learning provides a principled foundation for discovering reusable latent scientific concepts that can accelerate scientific interpretation across imaging domains.

title: Genetic dissection of DNA damage response pathways reveals divergent modulation of PD-1 blockade response in colorectal cancer
abstract: Although MSI-H/dMMR colorectal cancers and the rarer subset with pathogenic POLE exonuclease domain mutations can benefit from immune checkpoint blockade, MSS colorectal cancer remains largely refractory, raising the question of whether other DNA damage response defects may also confer sensitivity to immunotherapy. Here, we performed a systematic in vivo screen of recurrently altered DNA damage response (DDR) genes to determine whether distinct repair defects modulate response to PD-1 blockade in MSS colorectal cancer. Using a genome-edited murine model in immunocompetent mice, we found that DDR perturbations produced heterogeneous outcomes, indicating that the immunologic consequences of DNA repair deficiency may be pathway-specific. Loss of Brca1, Brca2, Atm, and Fanca enhanced response to anti-PD-1 therapy, whereas Atr and Msh6 deficiency were associated with poor benefit. Brca1/2-deficient tumors showed the strongest regressions, supporting a link between core homologous recombination deficiency and increased immune sensitivity. In an independent cohort of colorectal cancer patients treated with ICB from the MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort, BRCA1 alterations were associated with improved survival status, while FANCA alterations showed a similar trend. Because ATM is therapeutically targetable, we evaluated pharmacologic ATM inhibition in MSS colorectal cancer. Sustained ATM inhibition induced immune-related transcriptional programs in vitro and, when administered as a pre-treatment in vivo, enhanced the antitumor activity of PD-1 blockade. Together, these findings suggest that selected DDR alterations may represent candidate biomarkers of immunotherapy sensitivity, while ATM inhibition may provide a rational combination strategy to enhance PD-1 blockade in MSS colorectal cancer.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 Editing of Myeloid Lectins Reveals Target-Dependent Transcriptional Remodeling in Tumor-Associated Macrophages
abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) integrate multiple microenvironmental signals, including lectin-mediated recognition of tumor-associated glycans. Although several myeloid lectins have been implicated in tumor-macrophage interactions, their contributions to immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes remain poorly defined. We implemented a CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) workflow in primary human monocytes to enable comparative loss-of-function interrogation of five potentially immunosuppressive lectins we previously reported. CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery conditions were benchmarked in freshly isolated monocytes using CD14 as a technical target, followed by sgRNA editing efficiency screening for CLEC4E, CLEC6A, CD209, SELL, and SIGLEC9 in HeLa S3 cells. Selected guides were applied to primary monocytes before co-culture in a 3D model with BT474 breast cancer cells. Editing was quantified by Sanger-sequencing deconvolution, while co-culture-derived CD45+ macrophages were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting and characterized by bulk RNA sequencing. All five lectins were successfully perturbed, although gene editing efficiency remained target- and donor-dependent. Transcriptomic analysis revealed target-specific reprogramming and recurrent immunometabolic responses. mTORC1 signaling was consistently enriched, together with the remodeling of cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation. CLEC6A deletion achieved attenuation of hypoxia-, angiogenesis-, and TNF/NF-kB-associated programs. CD209 and SIGLEC9 deletion similarly reduced hypoxia- and angiogenesis-associated signatures while promoting lipid and oxidative metabolism. CLEC4E perturbation induced broad remodeling of lipid and oxidative metabolism and stress-response, despite comparatively limited editing efficiency. Comparative lectin perturbation thus identified CLEC6A as the strongest candidate for further mechanistic investigation, while CLEC4E showed broad transcriptional remodeling despite lower editing efficiency, supporting its prioritization for improved genetic interrogation. Responses to CD209 and SIGLEC9 targeting further support tumor glycan-myeloid signaling as a regulator of TAM state. Overall, lectin perturbation redirected TAM transcriptional states through distinct immunometabolic programs rather than a uniform pro-inflammatory polarization, highlighting lectin-dependent immunometabolic regulation as a promising axis for further investigation.

CLEC4E perturbation induced broad remodeling of lipid and oxidative metabolism and stress-response, despite comparatively limited editing efficiency. Comparative lectin perturbation thus identified CLEC6A as the strongest candidate for further mechanistic investigation, while CLEC4E showed broad transcriptional remodeling despite lower editing efficiency, supporting its prioritization for improved genetic interrogation. Responses to CD209 and SIGLEC9 targeting further support tumor glycan-myeloid signaling as a regulator of TAM state. Overall, lectin perturbation redirected TAM transcriptional states through distinct immunometabolic programs rather than a uniform pro-inflammatory polarization, highlighting lectin-dependent immunometabolic regulation as a promising axis for further investigation.
